title: Freedom of Speech and Political Activities by Foreigners in Singapore
what_it_is: Freedom of Speech and Political Activities by Foreigners in Singapore

sections.label: Laws on public speech
sections.summary: The Ministry says criminal and civil laws govern what people can and cannot say in public.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think her question relates to people expressing their views, that there was dishonesty, unpatriotic actions, and whether they should be allowed to say those things; and the Member has asked for the Ministry's views.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There are criminal, civil laws that govern what people can and cannot say in public.

sections.label: Online speech and POHA
sections.summary: The Protection from Harassment Act was strengthened a few months ago to let people take action.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And I think the Member will know that in the online space, people will say what they like.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We strengthened the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) a few months ago to allow people to take action and give individuals more power.

sections.label: Laws on foreign students' political activity
sections.summary: Laws including the Public Order Act set boundaries for political activities by foreigners.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Member also asked about the guidelines or laws under which foreign students may participate in student activities.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There are laws that set the boundaries for political activities by foreigners.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They include the Public Order Act and the Public Entertainments (Speakers' Corner) Exemption Order 2016 and other legislation.

sections.label: Students, security risks, monitoring
sections.summary: Engaging with student unions does not ipso facto make foreigners security risks, but they will be monitored if they do.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
sentences.text: In other words, would there be some kind of security risks, for example, to the students?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think there are two different issues being conflated here – whether they should be engaging with students and student unions, in the context of universities, I leave it to the Minister for Education.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That does not ipso facto mean that they become security risks.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If they do become security risks, they will be monitored.
